Hawaii Code AI-Thon: why make things (part 1 of 2)

You've had an idea for a classroom tool. A timer with sound. A partner shuffler. A standards tracker. Most of them never got built.

Before: writing the code used to be the work. You decide what to make, then the hard part, writing the code, hours of it, every bracket by hand, then you check whether it works. Both ends got rushed. Knowing what to make, and whether it worked, was always the point. But most of the effort got eaten by the middle.

After: now the judgment is the work. The AI generates the code, and that part is cheap now. The middle got cheap. What's left is the whole job now.

First: what are we making? Why? For whom? What counts as success? The AI can't answer these. You can.

Then: does it work? Testing is the important part now. A student tries the partner shuffler with 7 students and someone is left alone. The teacher asks for a group of three and tries it again with all 7. Only someone who knows the room catches that.

These are moves we already teach: define scope, name success, read the output skeptically. Your students watch the way you work. If you slot-machine it, they learn slot-machine. If you manage it like a project manager, they learn project management.

You don't need a CS degree, a budget line, or an IT ticket. You can just make digital things.
